newsitem.title: INDONESIA: FOCUS-Indonesia stocks, rupiah fall past barriers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Indonesia stocks, rupiah fall past barriers.

text.p: Indonesian stocks and the rupiah currency both fell through important psychological barriers to record lows on Monday, ignoring President Suharto's appeal to the markets to remain calm.

The rupiah fell briefly below the 3,000 level against the dollar but later recovered slightly to close in Jakarta at 2,970/80. That is a fall of almost 27 percent since the beginning of the year and about 25 percent since the beginning of July.

The stock market index dived 8.41 percent in the morning -- the biggest intra-day fall ever -- as investors panicked in the face of further weakness in the beleaguered rupiah, Friday's fall on Wall Street and increased margin calls.

A spurt of late buying, which some brokers ascribed to state brokerages, pushed the index back up, but it still finished at a closing low for the year of 599.64 points, down almost three percent and below the psychologically-important 600-point barrier.
"It's not only a black Monday, it's the blackest Monday," said Hengky Sumarli, the sales director of Amantara Securities, a local brokerage house.

"The main thing is the currency and the lack of confidence," said Stephen Rogers, head of research for UBS Securities, referring to the woes afflicting the stock market. "Everything else is a contributory fact."
Brokers pointed to increased margin calls, short-covering by local investors, high short-term interest rates and Friday's 247-point fall on the Dow Jones index as other reasons for the sell-off.
One currency trader said the rupiah, battered for weeks by speculators, was now at a "ridiculously low" level against the dollar.

"We have seen some offshore selling (of dollars)," said Edwin Png, the chief of the treasury department for Bank of America Jakarta, adding that local appetite for the U.S. currency was keeping the rupiah weak.
"Offshore parties think the rupiah is ridiculously low at this level. A lot of funds are looking for a level to sell (dollars)."
Dealers said many Indonesian corporates were scrambling to hedge uncovered foreign currency borrowings, but it was the wrong time to do so and was further weakening the currency.
Analysts said both the stock and currency markets appeared to have ignored Suharto's call on Saturday to remain calm.
Uncharacteristically, Suharto used an annual state-of-the-nation address to speak of concerns surrounding Indonesian markets and said the weakness in the rupiah was a temporary aberration.

"It is of a temporary nature and, with the appropriate policy and the calmness of domestic players, the exchange rate will find a new equilibrium in line with prevailing economic fundamentals," he said in a nationally televised broadcast.
Few analysts have doubted that Indonesia's fundamentals are sound, but they say that the speculative nature of the attacks on the rupiah have taken on a life of their own.

Meanwhile, the government acknowledged on Monday that it would not be able to stick to its six percent inflation target for the year because of the rupiah's weakness but said it would try to keep the rate under 10 percent.

"We have predicted inflation at around six percent this year but that is before the rupiah weakness. Because of current developments it is hard to get that level. That means inflation will be higher than our prediction," State Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita told reporters.
"We hope inflation will be in single digits," he added.
